title: Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the ceiling of a given key, defined as the smallest element greater than or equal to the key. If no such element exists, return minus one. Explain how binary search converges to the ceiling.
shortTitle: Ceiling of a Number (Smallest Element Greater Than or Equal to the Key)

s1_definition.profdef: Ceiling of a Number is a Modified Binary Search variant. The ceiling of a key is the smallest array element that is greater than or equal to the key. We binary-search, and when the middle element is smaller than the key we move right, otherwise we move left while remembering the position. When the window closes, the start pointer lands on the ceiling index, or past the end if the key is larger than every element.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, loan interest slabs are stored in an ascending array, and when Priya requests a loan amount that is not exactly a slab boundary, we must charge the next slab at or above her amount. We binary-search the slab list, and the first slab that is at least her amount is the ceiling we apply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search; when the key is above mid go right, otherwise go left, and the start pointer finally points at the smallest value greater than or equal to the key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Ceiling of a Number is a Modified Binary Search variant. The ceiling of a key is the smallest array element that is greater than or equal to the key. We binary-search, and when the middle element is smaller than the key we move right, otherwise we move left while remembering the position. When the window closes, the start pointer lands on the ceiling index, or past the end if the key is larger than every element.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, loan interest slabs are stored in an ascending array, and when Priya requests a loan amount that is not exactly a slab boundary, we must charge the next slab at or above her amount. We binary-search the slab list, and the first slab that is at least her amount is the ceiling we apply.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search; when the key is above mid go right, otherwise go left, and the start pointer finally points at the smallest value greater than or equal to the key.

sections.s2_technical:
We handle the easy edge case first: if the key is greater than the last element there is no ceiling, so we return minus one. Otherwise we binary-search with `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. In the loop, `mid = start + (end - start) / 2`; if `key < arr[mid]` we set `end = mid - 1`, if `key > arr[mid]` we set `start = mid + 1`, and if equal we return `mid`. When the loop ends with `start > end`, the `start` index points to the smallest element greater than or equal to the key, so we return `arr[start]` (or its index, depending on the required output).

The reason `start` lands on the ceiling is that every time we move `end` left we keep the window of candidates that are at least the key, and every time we move `start` right we discard elements smaller than the key. For example, in array 1, 3, 8, 10, 15 with key 5, the search narrows until `start` points at 8, the ceiling.

A senior nuance is that the symmetric problem, the floor, which is the largest element less than or equal to the key, is solved identically except that `end` lands on the floor index. Recognising the start-ends-on-ceiling and end-ends-on-floor invariant is the key insight. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores interest-rate slab thresholds in an ascending array, and when Priya requests a loan amount that falls between two slabs, policy requires charging the next slab at or above her amount. This is exactly how the ceiling works: we need the smallest threshold greater than or equal to her amount.

Problem 2 — Scanning the slabs linearly is wasteful when there are many slabs. This is why we binary-search so the ceiling is found in logarithmic time, and we return minus one when the amount exceeds every slab, signalling a special-case escalation.

The code defines a `SlabService` exposing `ceilingSlab(slabs, amount)` returning the ceiling threshold or minus one. A `Demo` finds the slab applied to Priya's requested amount and logs it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: slabs 100000, 300000, 500000, 1000000 and amount 420000.

Step 1: 420000 is not greater than the last slab 1000000, so a ceiling exists and we proceed.

Step 2: start is 0, end is 3, mid is 1, slab at 1 is 300000, and 420000 is greater so start becomes 2.

Step 3: start is 2, end is 3, mid is 2, slab at 2 is 500000, and 420000 is less so end becomes 1.

Step 4: now start is 2 and end is 1, the loop ends, and start points at index 2 which holds 500000, the ceiling we charge Priya.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  slabs:[100000,300000,500000,1000000], amount=420000
    │
    ▼
  amount > last slab ? → no → continue
    │
    ▼
  binary search
    ├─ amount < mid → end = mid-1  (keep candidates >= amount)
    ├─ amount > mid → start = mid+1 (discard smaller)
    └─ equal        → return mid
    ▼
  start lands on ceiling → 500000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Ceiling of a Number is a Modified Binary Search variant where I find the smallest array element that is greater than or equal to the key. I first short-circuit the case where the key is larger than the last element, since then no ceiling exists and I return minus one. Otherwise I binary-search: when the key is below the middle element I move the end pointer left, when it is above I move the start pointer right, and on an exact match I return immediately.

The elegant part is the invariant that when the loop finishes with start past end, the start pointer is sitting exactly on the ceiling. That is because moving end left always preserves candidates at or above the key while moving start right discards everything smaller. The mirror problem, the floor, is identical except the end pointer lands on the answer, and knowing both invariants together is what demonstrates real command of the pattern.

At the National Bank of India I used this to apply interest-rate slabs: when Priya requested a loan amount sitting between two slab thresholds, policy required charging the next slab at or above her amount, which is precisely the ceiling. I binary-searched the ascending slab table so the correct slab was found in logarithmic time, and returned minus one to trigger an escalation when the amount exceeded every slab. Explaining the start-lands-on-ceiling invariant and the symmetric floor case is what shows an interviewer I truly understand the convergence.
